claim: Sleep is an essential behavioral state.
source: Sleep is an essential behavioral state.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific consensus about sleep.

claim: Sleep is induced by conserved sleep-active neurons that express GABA.
source: It is induced by conserved sleep-active neurons that express GABA.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: The transcription factor LIM-6 specifies GABAergic function.
source: the transcription factor LIM-6, which specifies GABAergic function
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and results sections.

claim: LIM-6 determines sleep neuron function through the expression of APTF-1.
source: the transcription factor LIM-6, which specifies GABAergic function, in parallel determines sleep neuron function through the expression of APTF-1
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that LIM-6 controls APTF-1 expression in RIS.

claim: APTF-1 specifies the expression of FLP-11 neuropeptides.
source: APTF-1, which specifies the expression of FLP-11 neuropeptides
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional profiling and reporter gene expression data.

claim: FLP-11, and not GABA, is the major component that determines the sleep-promoting function of RIS.
source: Surprisingly FLP-11, and not GABA, is the major component that determines the sleep-promoting function of RIS.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral analysis of flp-11 mutants and optogenetic experiments.

claim: FLP-11 is constantly expressed in RIS.
source: FLP-11 is constantly expressed in RIS.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing constant expression during sleep-wake cycles.

claim: At sleep onset RIS depolarizes and releases FLP-11 to induce a systemic sleep state.
source: At sleep onset RIS depolarizes and releases FLP-11 to induce a systemic sleep state.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging showing RIS activation at sleep onset and behavioral data.

claim: Sleep is defined by behavioral criteria such as an increased arousal threshold, reversibility, and homeostatic regulation.
source: Sleep is a systemic physiological state that is defined by behavioral criteria such as an increased arousal threshold, reversibility, and homeostatic regulation (Campbell and Tobler, 1984).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Campbell and Tobler, 1984.

claim: Sleep behavior has been found in all animals that have a nervous system and that have been studied thoroughly.
source: Sleep behavior has been found in all animals that have a nervous system and that have been studied thoroughly (Cirelli and Tononi, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cirelli and Tononi, 2008.

claim: Sleep homeostasis suggests that sleep is vital for animal life.
source: Sleep homeostasis suggests that sleep is vital for animal life
evidence: This is an inference based on the concept of homeostatic regulation.

claim: Deprivation of sleep typically has detrimental consequences.
source: deprivation of this behavior typically has detrimental consequences (Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rechtschaffen and Bergmann, 1995.

claim: In mammals, wake and sleep are controlled by two antagonistic systems.
source: In mammals, wake and sleep are controlled by two antagonistic systems.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: The ascending system is wake-promoting.
source: The ascending system is wake-promoting (Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949; Starzl et al., 1951)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moruzzi and Magoun, 1949 and Starzl et al., 1951.

claim: The descending system is sleep-promoting.
source: the descending system is sleep-promoting (von Economo, 1930; Nauta, 1946; McGinty and Sterman, 1968; McGinty et al., 2004; Saper et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sleep-active neurons are located in the preoptic area (VLPO and MnPO), the parafacial zone of the medulla, and the thalamic reticular nucleus.
source: Central to the control of sleep are sleep-active sleep-promoting neurons such as those located in the preoptic area (Ventral Lateral Preoptic Nucleus, VLPO and Median Preoptic Nucleus, MnPO), the parafacial zone of the medulla, and the thalamic reticular nucleus (McGinty et al., 2004; Anaclet et al., 2012; 2014; Alam et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sleep-active neurons typically fire preferentially at the onset of sleep.
source: These neurons typically fire preferentially at the onset of sleep
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep-active neurons actively induce sleep.
source: they actively induce sleep
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Sleep-active neurons express the neurotransmitter GABA.
source: they express the neurotransmitter GABA
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The VLPO also expresses the neuropeptide Galanin.
source: The VLPO also expresses the neuropeptide Galanin (Sherin et al., 1998; Szymusiak et al., 1998; Gaus et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sherin et al., 1998; Szymusiak et al., 1998; Gaus et al., 2002.

claim: Small brain areas can induce the global state of sleep that affects all areas of the brain and also other organs.
source: Interestingly, small brain areas can induce the global state of sleep that affects all areas of the brain and also other organs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sleep regulation.

claim: Sleep neurons induce sleep through projections to arousal centers.
source: It has been proposed that sleep neurons induce sleep through projections to arousal centers (Saper et al., 2005; Sherin et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Saper et al., 2005 and Sherin et al., 1996.

claim: The ascending and descending systems mutually inhibit each other in a flip-flop switch.
source: To ensure that sleep and wake are manifested as discrete states, the ascending and descending systems mutually inhibit each other in a flip-flop switch (Gallopin et al., 2000; Saper et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gallopin et al., 2000 and Saper et al., 2001.

claim: C. elegans has an invariant nervous system of just 302 neurons.
source: has a small and invariant nervous system of just 302 neurons
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy supported by citations.

claim: C. elegans is transparent.
source: it is transparent (Brenner, 1974; White et al., 1986; Chalfie et al., 1994)
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans supported by citations.

claim: Quiescence behavior in C. elegans can be found in satiated adults, after stress, during dauer diapause, and during larval development.
source: In C. elegans, quiescence behavior can be found in satiated adults, after stress, during dauer diapause, and during larval development (Cassada and Russell, 1975; You et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cassada and Russell, 1975; You et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2014.

claim: Developmentally controlled sleep in C. elegans can be found in larvae prior to each of the four molts.
source: Here, we focus on a well-characterized developmentally controlled sleep behavior that can be found in C. elegans larvae prior to each of the four molts (Cassada and Russell, 1975).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cassada and Russell, 1975.

claim: Developmentally controlled sleep fulfills the criteria that define sleep in other organisms.
source: Developmentally controlled sleep fulfills the criteria that define sleep in other organisms (Raizen et al., 2008; Trojanowski and Raizen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Raizen et al., 2008 and Trojanowski and Raizen, 2016.

claim: The criteria for sleep are reversibility, an increased arousal threshold, and homeostatic regulation.
source: These criteria are reversibility, an increased arousal threshold, and homeostatic regulation (Raizen et al., 2008; Jeon et al., 1999; Schwarz et al., 2011; Driver et al., 2013; Iwanir et al., 2013; Nagy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sleep behavior in C. elegans and sleep in other organisms are controlled by homologous genes.
source: Further analysis has shown that sleep behavior in C. elegans and sleep in other organisms are controlled by homologous genes such as period/lin-42, Notch signaling, EGF signaling and several other molecules including neurotransmitter systems (Nagy et al., 2014; Monsalve et al., 2011; Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2007; Singh et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Sleep behavior in C. elegans and sleep in other organisms share a common evolutionary origin.
source: These molecular similarities suggest that sleep behavior in C. elegans and sleep in other organisms share a common evolutionary origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular similarities.

claim: Sleep behavior in C. elegans profoundly changes the activity of neurons and muscles.
source: Sleep behavior in C. elegans has been shown to profoundly change the activity of neurons and muscles (Schwarz et al., 2011; Iwanir et al., 2013; Cho and Sternberg, 2014; Schwarz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schwarz et al., 2011; Iwanir et al., 2013; Cho and Sternberg, 2014; Schwarz et al., 2012.

claim: Sleep behavior in C. elegans requires the activity of the single interneuron RIS.
source: It requires the activity of the single interneuron RIS (neuron class of one ring interneuron; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: RIS is active at the onset of sleep.
source: This neuron is active at the onset of sleep
evidence: This is supported by prior research and data in this manuscript.

claim: RIS actively induces sleep.
source: it actively induces sleep
evidence: This is supported by prior research and data in this manuscript.

claim: RIS expresses GABA.
source: it expresses GABA (Turek et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turek et al., 2013.

claim: RIS is similar to sleep-active neurons in mammals.
source: Thus, RIS is similar to sleep-active neurons in mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on shared characteristics.

claim: RIS requires APTF-1 to be sleep-inducing.
source: In order to be sleep-inducing, RIS requires APTF-1, a highly conserved transcription factor of the AP2 family.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: APTF-1 is a highly conserved transcription factor of the AP2 family.
source: APTF-1, a highly conserved transcription factor of the AP2 family
evidence: This is established knowledge about APTF-1.

claim: Without APTF-1, RIS is still sleep-active but can no longer induce sleep.
source: Without APTF-1, RIS is still sleep-active but can no longer induce sleep (Turek et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turek et al., 2013.

claim: Mutation in the AP2 homolog TFAP2beta causes Char syndrome in humans.
source: In humans, mutation in the AP2 homolog TFAP2beta causes Char syndrome, which is linked to insomnia or sleepwalking (Mani et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mani et al., 2005.

claim: Char syndrome is linked to insomnia or sleepwalking.
source: Char syndrome, which is linked to insomnia or sleepwalking (Mani et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mani et al., 2005.

claim: Sleep-neurons and AP2 transcription factors are conserved regulators of sleep.
source: Together, this supports the view that sleep-neurons and AP2 transcription factors are conserved regulators of sleep.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented and cited research.

claim: lim-6 mutants had strongly reduced or even complete absence of immobility during the non-pumping phase.
source: The mutants had strongly reduced or even complete absence of immobility during the non-pumping phase (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RIS activity increased at sleep onset in wild-type animals.
source: We found that RIS activity increased at sleep onset in wild-type animals
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: RIS activity normally increased in lim-6 mutants during the time the animal should enter sleep.
source: also normally increased in lim-6 mutants during the time the animal should enter sleep (Figure 1B)
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: aptf-1 expression was completely abolished in most individuals and strongly reduced in the remaining ones in all developmental stages in lim-6 mutants.
source: aptf-1 expression was completely abolished in most individuals and strongly reduced in the remaining ones in all developmental stages (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: aptf-1 did not control the expression of unc-25 or the vesicular GABA transporter gene unc-47.
source: We also looked at GABAergic function in aptf-1 mutant worms and found that aptf-1 did not control the expression of unc-25 or the vesicular GABA transporter gene unc-47 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LIM-6 does not appear to affect sleep primarily through GABAergic function determination.
source: Thus, LIM-6 does not appear to affect sleep primarily through GABAergic function determination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that APTF-1 does not control GABAergic markers.

claim: LIM-6 controls sleep-promoting function primarily through a parallel pathway that depends on APTF-1.
source: Rather, LIM-6 controls sleep-promoting function primarily through a parallel pathway that depends on APTF-1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing separate control of GABAergic and sleep-promoting functions.

claim: flp-11 was strongly downregulated in aptf-1 mutant worms in both embryos and larvae.
source: The microarray experiment revealed that flp-11, a neuropeptide gene, was strongly downregulated in aptf-1 mutant worms in both embryos and larvae (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1, Table 1A and 1B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptional profiling data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: flp-11 was expressed strongly in RIS and faintly in a few additional neurons.
source: flp-11 was expressed strongly in RIS and faintly in a few additional neurons.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data.

claim: flp-11 expression was abolished or greatly reduced in RIS in aptf-1 mutant worms.
source: Expression was abolished or greatly reduced in RIS in aptf-1 mutant worms (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: mKate2 was constantly expressed during larval development both during sleep and wake.
source: We followed the expression of flp-11:mKate2 over the sleep-wake rhythm and found that mKate2 was constantly expressed during larval development both during sleep and wake (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of mouse tfap2beta partially restored immobility in aptf-1 mutants.
source: Nose speed measurements during sleep showed that tfap2beta expression partially restored immobility (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Expression of mouse tfap2beta partially restored the expression of flp-11 in aptf-1 mutant worms.
source: Expression of mouse tfap2beta also partially restored the expression of flp-11 in aptf-1 mutant worms (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The binding site of AP2 is conserved over 600 million years of bilaterian evolution.
source: In fact, it has been shown that the binding site of AP2 is conserved over 600 million years of bilaterian evolution, and the different mammalian AP2 paralogs have nearly identical binding sites (Nitta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nitta et al., 2015.

claim: A putative AP2-binding site was found in the flp-11 promoter region.
source: Thus, we searched for mammalian AP2 transcription factors binding sites in the promoter region of flp-11 (Eckert et al., 2005; Grant et al., 2011). Indeed, we found a putative AP2-binding site in the flp-11 promoter region, consistent with the regulation of flp-11 by aptf-1 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: aptf-1 is required for flp-11 expression in RIS.
source: These results show that aptf-1 is required for flp-11 expression in RIS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: flp-11 mutant larvae showed a normal pre-molting cessation of pumping.
source: flp-11 mutant larvae showed a normal pre-molting cessation of pumping.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations.

claim: Locomotion quiescence was strongly reduced in flp-11 mutant larvae.
source: However, locomotion quiescence was strongly reduced in flp-11 mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: Nose immobility was 48% in wild type and less than 14% in flp-11 mutants.
source: Although nose immobility was 48% in wild type, it was strongly reduced to less than 14% in flp-11 mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A wild-type copy of flp-11 could rescue the flp-11 mutant phenotype.
source: We found that the wild-type transgene could rescue the flp-11 mutant phenotype (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of flp-11 in aptf-1 mutants partially restored immobility.
source: Whereas aptf-1 mutants without the transgene did not show any detectable immobility, the flp-11 transgene partially restored immobility (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RIS strongly activated at the onset of the non-pumping period in flp-11 mutant worms.
source: RIS strongly activated at the onset of the non-pumping period in flp-11 mutant worms (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: flp-11 is not required for activation of RIS at sleep onset.
source: Thus, flp-11 is not required for activation of RIS at sleep onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the calcium imaging data.

claim: Wild-type animals showed a reduction in movement and became immobile after blue light illumination during optogenetic activation of RIS.
source: Although wild-type animals showed a reduction in movement and became immobile after blue light illumination
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experimental data.

claim: flp-11 mutant worms did not decrease their movement but rather increased it during optogenetic activation of RIS.
source: flp-11 mutant worms did not decrease their movement but rather increased it (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Adult worms expressing FLP-11 driven by the heat shock promoter became immobile 1–2 hr after the heat shock.
source: Adult worms that were expressing FLP-11 driven by the heat shock promoter became immobile 1–2 hr after the heat shock.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from heat shock experiments.

claim: Control worms that were heat shocked but did not express the transgene or expressed other flp genes did not show any immobilization.
source: Control worms that were heat shocked but did not express the transgene or expressed other flp genes did not show any immobilization (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RIS induces sleep through FLP-11.
source: Taken together these data imply that RIS induces sleep through FLP-11.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: FLP-11 peptides are expressed in RIS during both sleep and wake.
source: These peptides are expressed in RIS during both sleep and wake
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data showing constant expression.

claim: Optogenetic activation of RIS can induce quiescence during wake.
source: optogenetic activation of RIS can induce quiescence during wake
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic experimental data.

claim: RIS can induce sleep at any time.
source: This suggests a model in which RIS can induce sleep at any time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the constant expression of FLP-11 and optogenetic data.

claim: RIS depolarizes at sleep onset.
source: According to this model, RIS depolarizes at sleep onset
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data.

claim: RIS releases FLP-11 at sleep onset, which then induces sleep.
source: This triggers FLP-11 release, which in turn systemically induces sleep behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and the proposed model.

claim: The maximum quiescence induced by FLP-11 overexpression was reduced in each of the receptor mutants (FRPR-3, NPR-4, and NPR-22).
source: We found that the maximum quiescence was reduced in each of these mutants, albeit only slightly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The triple mutant containing all three receptor deletions had the strongest reduction in quiescence.
source: the triple mutant had the strongest reduction in quiescence (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The quiescence induced by FLP-11 overexpression partly depends on multiple effectors.
source: Thus, the quiescence induced by FLP-11 overexpression partly depends on multiple effectors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the receptor mutant data.

claim: The single receptor mutants did not show a significant reduction in immobility.
source: Whereas the single receptor mutants did not show a significant reduction in immobility
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data.

claim: The receptor triple mutant showed a small increase in nose speed during sleep and a small reduction of immobility.
source: the receptor triple mutant showed a small increase in nose speed during sleep and a small reduction of immobility (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FRPR-3 expressed in approximately 30 neurons, mostly in the head.
source: The promoter fusions showed that FRPR-3 expressed in approximately 30 neurons, mostly in the head.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data.

claim: NPR-4 expressed in five neurons.
source: NPR-4 expressed in five neurons (Cohen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data and a citation to Cohen et al., 2009.

claim: NPR-22 expressed in several neurons, muscle tissue in the pharynx and in the head.
source: NPR-22 expressed in several neurons, muscle tissue in the pharynx and in the head (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The receptors were expressed in neurons that are not postsynaptic to RIS, with the exception of the AVK neuron.
source: Interestingly, the receptors were expressed in neurons that are not postsynaptic to RIS (White et al., 1986). The only exception that we found was the AVK neuron, which is postsynaptic to RIS and expressed FRPR-3.
evidence: This is supported by reporter gene expression data and anatomical knowledge from White et al., 1986.

claim: FRPR-3 and NPR-4 were weakly expressed and localized mostly to the nerve ring.
source: Translational fusions showed that FRPR-3 and NPR-4 were weakly expressed and localized mostly to the nerve ring
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging of translational fusions.

claim: NPR-22 was localized broadly to the plasma membrane of neurons, and muscles of the pharynx, head, and muscle.
source: whereas NPR-22 was localized broadly to the plasma membrane of neurons, and muscles of the pharynx, head, and muscle (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The phenotypes for the GPCRs observed were small and the binding affinities of FLP-11 peptides to these GPCRs in vitro were low.
source: The phenotypes for the GPCRs that we observed were small and the binding affinities of FLP-11 peptides to these GPCRs in vitro were low which makes it premature to conclude that these receptors act by binding of FLP-11 (Frooninckx et al., 2012; Mertens et al., 2004; 2006; Cohen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on the experimental data and citations to in vitro binding studies.

claim: FLP-11 could act through one main receptor, which remains unidentified.
source: It could be that FLP-11 acts through one main receptor, which remains unidentified.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: FLP-11 could act through several redundant receptors, which may include FRPR-3, NPR-4, and NPR-22.
source: Alternatively, FLP-11 could act through several redundant receptors, which may include FRPR-3, NPR-4, and NPR-22.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: GABA has been proposed to play a major role in sleep function.
source: GABA has been proposed to play a major role in sleep function.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Enhancers of GABAergic neurotransmission have been used to treat sleeping problems.
source: Enhancers of GABAergic neurotransmission have been used to treat sleeping problems
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: GABA has been suggested to play a role in sleep induction in several systems including C. elegans.
source: GABA has been suggested to play a role in sleep induction in several systems including C. elegans (Singh et al., 2014; Dabbish and Raizen, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Dabbish and Raizen, 2011.

claim: The authors did not find evidence that GABA is the major sleep-inducing transmitter in RIS.
source: In contrast to the common view that GABA is the major sleep inducer in sleep-active neurons, we did not find evidence that GABA is the major sleep-inducing transmitter in RIS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Optogenetic activation of RIS still causes quiescence in unc-25 mutant worms.
source: This is consistent with our previous observation that optogenetic activation of RIS still causes quiescence in unc-25 mutant worms
evidence: This is supported by a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: unc-25 mutant worms still show sleeping behavior.
source: unc-25 mutant worms still show sleeping behavior (Turek et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Turek et al., 2013.

claim: GABAergic function induction can be separated from sleep neuron function downstream of lim-6.
source: In addition, here we show that GABAergic function induction can be separated from sleep neuron function downstream of lim-6.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: GABA plays a rather minor role in sleep-induction in RIS.
source: This suggests that GABA plays a rather minor role in sleep-induction in RIS and that we did not detect it.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: FLP-11 is a crucial sleep-inducing component in RIS.
source: Our results show that FLP-11 is a crucial sleep-inducing component in RIS
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: FLP-11 is an important target of aptf-1.
source: FLP-11 is a crucial sleep-inducing component in RIS and an important target of aptf-1
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Sleep neurons of the VLPO express the inhibitory neuropeptide Galanin.
source: In mammals, sleep neurons of the VLPO express the inhibitory neuropeptide Galanin, and projections extend to the tuberomammillary nucleus, which expresses Galanin receptors (Sherin et al., 1998; Gaus et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sherin et al., 1998 and Gaus et al., 2002.

claim: VLPO projections extend to the tuberomammillary nucleus, which expresses Galanin receptors.
source: projections extend to the tuberomammillary nucleus, which expresses Galanin receptors (Sherin et al., 1998; Gaus et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sherin et al., 1998 and Gaus et al., 2002.

claim: The locus coeruleus is innervated by VLPO projections and can be inhibited by Galanin administration.
source: The locus coeruleus, a wake-promoting brain region, is also innervated by VLPO projections and can be inhibited by Galanin administration (Seutin et al., 1989; Pieribone et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seutin et al., 1989 and Pieribone et al., 1995.

claim: Galanin has been shown to have sedating effects on both zebrafish and human subjects.
source: Also, Galanin has been shown to have sedating effects on both zebrafish and human subjects (Woods et al., 2014; Murck et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Woods et al., 2014 and Murck et al., 2004.

claim: Sleep phenotypes for Galanin knockouts have not been reported, despite being available for several years.
source: However, sleep phenotypes for Galanin knockouts have not been reported, despite being available for several years (Wynick et al., 1998; Kerr et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wynick et al., 1998 and Kerr et al., 2000.

claim: Galanin has a modulatory role on sleep, but may not be central to sleep induction.
source: These experiments suggest that Galanin has a modulatory role on sleep, but may not be central to sleep induction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature.

claim: Galanin does not appear to be homologous to FLP-11.
source: Galanin does not appear to be homologous to FLP-11, as it belongs to the family of Galanin peptides (Lang et al., 2007), whereas flp-11 encodes peptides of the RFamide family (Li et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on citations to Lang et al., 2007 and Li et al., 1999.

claim: Galanin is expressed widely in the brain and has diverse functions.
source: Also, unlike FLP-11, Galanin is expressed widely in the brain and has diverse functions (Maria Vrontakis, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maria Vrontakis, 2002.

claim: In Drosophila, sleep requires a neuropeptide called sNPF.
source: In Drosophila, sleep requires a neuropeptide called sNPF, which may be functionally similar to FLP-11 as both are inhibitory and are released from sleep-promoting neurons (Shang et al., 2013; Vecsey et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shang et al., 2013; Vecsey et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013.

claim: sNPF may be functionally similar to FLP-11 as both are inhibitory and are released from sleep-promoting neurons.
source: which may be functionally similar to FLP-11 as both are inhibitory and are released from sleep-promoting neurons (Shang et al., 2013; Vecsey et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013)
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Shang et al., 2013; Vecsey et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibitory neuropeptides appear to play important roles in sleep-promoting neurons across species.
source: Thus, inhibitory neuropeptides appear to play important roles in sleep-promoting neurons across species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and cited literature.

claim: The transcription factor LIM-6 separately controls GABAergic and sleep-promoting functions.
source: In this model, the transcription factor LIM-6 separately controls GABAergic and sleep-promoting functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Sleep-promoting function is mediated by the expression of the APTF-1 transcription factor.
source: Sleep-promoting function is mediated by the expression of the APTF-1 transcription factor
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: APTF-1 is crucially required for sleep induction by RIS.
source: which is crucially required for sleep induction by RIS
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: APTF-1 is required for the expression of sleep-inducing FLP-11 peptides.
source: APTF-1, in turn, is required for the expression of sleep-inducing FLP-11 peptides.
